title: Proof The Code Got Better
eyebrow: One command now says whether a change left the codebase better or worse than it found it, and refuses the change if it made it worse. Every number it turns on was measured off this codebase, and every rule has been shown red with the fault put back.

actions.fyi: Built and running. Nothing is needed from you. Six rules refuse a change on their own; the run is green on the codebase as it stands, so nothing is blocked today. Three files are excused by name because they already hold two unrelated things each, and splitting them is separate work you can order or leave.

content.label: What you have now
content.lead: One command, six rules. It reads the tree as it stands, or any earlier point of it, without disturbing anyone else's work.

tiles.key: faults found, four of them in the rules themselves
files excused, each owned by a ticket

rows.title: A copy edited on one side only
rows.note: The thing you named. Two stretches of code that say the same thing, and a change that reaches into one of them and not the other. Judged on the tree as it stood before the change, because a reading taken afterwards is missing exactly the pairs the edit pushed apart

rows.title: A number written out in two languages
rows.note: Nothing in the build makes a value in the code and the same value in a surface-colouring program agree. They agree because somebody typed both. Rewriting one side alone is refused

rows.title: A crossing the design forbids
rows.note: The drawn map of which part may reach which, compared against the one the code actually builds. The crossings that stand today are listed with the ticket that owns each, and that list may only ever shrink

rows.title: Parts that depend on each other in a ring
rows.note: Code that can only be understood all at once is where defects gather. Folder hubs are set aside first, or the ordinary shape of this project reads as one giant ring

rows.title: A file that has quietly become two
rows.note: Not length. A part of a file that nothing else in the file talks to, heavy enough to be a file on its own, is a file that has not been given a name yet

rows.title: A quiet run bought by deleting tests
rows.note: Every other rule can be silenced by deleting the thing it names. The amount of behaviour standing under a check may rise and may not fall — the one rule with no threshold to derive

content.label: What building it found
content.lead: Four faults, none of them looked for. Each was found by running the measurement rather than by reading the code.

blocks.label: Two picture checks compare against nothing and report success
blocks.text: The reflection, shadow and blocked-light checks are the same body pasted three times. Each ends by demanding that the affected pixels moved more than the unaffected ones, and either group can come out empty. An empty group reads as did-not-move rather than as no-data, so the comparison quietly turns into a did-it-draw-anything test. Blocked-light guards both groups, shadow guards one, reflection guards the other. This is the fault the whole job was built to catch, and looking for it is what turned it up.

blocks.label: One of my own rules was blind to the worst version of its own fault
blocks.text: The rule that pairs a number written in two languages read the tree afterwards through the same filter it uses to choose pairs — values written in both. So a value taken out of one language entirely disappeared from the reading and there was nothing left to compare. Removing one of nine copies was caught; removing the last one was not. Found on the first run of the check that breaks each rule on purpose, which is the whole argument for having that check.

blocks.label: Three files hold two unrelated things each
blocks.text: One of them keeps picture decoding beside finding the sun in a photograph of the sky — two subjects with nothing to say to each other, under one name. The other two are a table of drawing setups and a test file. All three are excused by name so the rule is quiet today, each pinned to a ticket, and the list of excuses may only ever shrink.

blocks.label: The lock that stops two sessions merging at once refused a session its own lock
blocks.text: A session works in two places — it takes the lock in its own copy of the work and merges from the shared one — and the gate compared the lock's holder against a name derived from wherever the merge was run. So it told the holder it did not hold it and queued it behind everyone. Reported and already fixed by the session that owns that machinery.

content.label: Read by someone who did not write it
content.lead: The job cannot close until a reader who did not build it has been through it. It found nine things, all of them real. Every one is fixed and landed.

rows: Nothing in the project ever ran any of it, so six rules that can refuse a change refused nothing anybody would see
Two tests in the gate that runs on every change: one runs the rules, one runs the fault injections
Removing one of two copies — the ordinary way to fix duplication — was refused as abandoning a twin
Removal is told from abandonment by length: an edit leaves a stretch as long as it was, taking it out does not
Asking to compare against a named earlier point still judged the change against a different one, so a worsening already committed read as clean
The point you name is the point it measures from
Folding two hand-typed copies of a number into one was refused as though the number had been rewritten
Fewer copies is tidying up. It wants a different number in their place, not fewer
A file already failing was blamed on the current change whenever a size inside the message moved
A standing failure is recognised by rule and file, never by its wording
The rule against deleting tests could not see the build tooling — where every one of these rules is written
It counts the tooling too, and the injections fail outright if any rule has no case at all
Three smaller ones: two comments pointing at sections that never existed, a run leaving throwaway copies on disk, and a report going silent after its first failure
All three fixed; the pointer check now reads the build tooling, which is how the first two got in

blocks.label: Fixing them found two more
blocks.text: The rule against deleting tests only noticed when the whole codebase lost ground, so two checks added by the same change covered one deleted somewhere else — it asks per file now. And the first attempt at telling removal from abandonment asked whether any window of the deleted code still appeared in the file, which fails in exactly the repetitive files where duplication lives.

content.label: Shown to have teeth
content.lead: A rule that passes proves nothing — the code it read may simply have been clean. Each rule is shown refusing the fault it exists for, and shown letting the honest version of the same edit through. This runs as a check, so it keeps being true.

rows: One number changed inside a stretch four test files carry word for word
Refused, naming all four files and both ends of every pair
Quiet
A value rewritten in the code and left alone in the surface-colouring program
Refused, naming where it still stands
Quiet

Refused, naming the part and what it reached

blocks.label: The comparison judges places, not numbers
blocks.text: A number moving says how big the codebase is, not how bad it is — the count of watched pairs, the count of parts, every size count all rise on ordinary work and were being read as a decline. What decides now is a place refused now and not refused before, printed as the rule, the file, and the rule's own sentence. A codebase already failing stays failing either way; this says whether your change is what made it so.

content.label: Where the numbers come from
content.lead: You told me my own numbers were guesses. They were — five of seven. Every one of them is now read off this codebase, and every one can be re-read with a single command.

rows: How long a stretch has to be to count as a copy
A whole routine here runs about a hundred tokens, and below sixty, matches start appearing between two halves of the tree that share no logic at all — a false-alarm rate measured rather than assumed
How alike two copies must be before a change is refused over them
Twenty real changes replayed: none refused at this bar, two refused one bar looser
How common a repeated pattern may be before it is set aside
The setting inherited from the textbook was hiding a third of the real findings while reporting only that it had skipped something
How heavy a part of a file must be to count as a file
What a file weighs here — half of them are under this. Six points sampled across the last four hundred changes: one file ever crossed it, and it is long gone
How much behaviour must stand under a check
No threshold at all. It is a direction: it may rise and may not fall. None of the last thirty changes lowered it

blocks.label: The measuring stick just got seventeen percent shorter
blocks.text: What makes the copy numbers measurable rather than assumed is that half the tree — the build tooling — shares no logic with the game, so any text the two agree on is a coincidence, and counting those gives a false-alarm rate off this codebase. That half has just shrunk, because the shared board machinery moved out to its own home. The numbers are not invalidated; the reading already scales by how many chances each side has. But they were read against a body seventeen percent larger than the one standing now, and they should be re-read rather than assumed when it changes again.

content.label: What it does not see
content.lead: Stated so a quiet run is not mistaken for a clean codebase.

items: A file that is two things is usually missed, not caught. Two halves that share enough vocabulary read as one thing — of ninety deliberate attempts to hide one whole subsystem inside another file, twenty-eight were caught.
Only the game and the build tooling are read. Content, scenes and documents are not.
The reading is by words, not by grammar. No rule may rest on the code having been understood.
Nothing runs against the network, so the answer is the same offline and a year from now — at the price of two otherwise good checks that need to fetch a list.

decisions.title: It measures the change, not the codebase
decisions.why: An absolute score is a number nobody can act on and every codebase fails. What is useful is whether this change made something worse than it found it, named to the file that did it.

decisions.title: How much code is duplicated is not measured at all
decisions.why: Measured here at fourteen percent and hand-checked: two thirds of it is unrelated code that happens to look alike. The strongest published study, using real bug records, found copied code carries fewer faults than the code around it. Only copies pulling apart are refused.

decisions.title: File length is a statistic, never a rule
decisions.why: Your ruling, and the measurement agrees flatly. Our longest files are single coherent things; a seventy-line file splits into three unrelated pieces. The principled replacement is whether a file holds one concern, which is length-blind.

decisions.title: Every ratio gets an absolute floor beside it
decisions.why: Almost every quality number in the field has code size underneath, so deleting code — including tests — improves all of them at once. Without floors this suite would reward deletion.

decisions.title: Loops are judged with folder hubs set aside
decisions.why: Run raw, a third of the codebase appears to be one giant loop, and it is the ordinary shape of the folder pattern this project prescribes. That version of the rule would be ignored within a week. Set the hubs aside and nine real ones remain.

decisions.title: History-based signals report and never refuse
decisions.why: They are the only ones dodgeable by changing how work is committed rather than what is written. Also measured: run on their own they call half the codebase drifted, almost all of it noise. They are only trustworthy chained to something read out of the code itself.

decisions.title: Five well-known measures were left out
decisions.why: A single maintainability score, whose formula was fitted once in 1994 against people's opinions and quietly retuned by every tool since. The classic object-oriented measures, which need a shape this codebase does not have. And a community-detection score that changes its answer with a parameter nobody can justify.

decisions.title: The structure map is built here rather than bought
decisions.why: No maintained tool produces one usable for this. The known weakness — wildcard imports it cannot follow — was measured before committing: sixteen cases in two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven, all listed.

decisions.title: Nothing runs against the network
decisions.why: Two otherwise good checks — known vulnerabilities and out-of-date dependencies — need to fetch a list. Left out so the suite gives the same answer offline and a year from now.

decisions.title: Drift is built first, boundaries second, comparison last
decisions.why: You let the recommended order stand. Drift is the thing you named, it is the thing that just turned up a live bug, and it is the only one of the three that pays back the day it lands — the same run that guards the future hands over a ranked list of what has already gone wrong.

decisions.title: Building the meter is not fixing what it reads
decisions.why: The five faults the measurement already turned up — the picture check that passes without looking, the two guards that check less than their names claim, the colour numbers kept in two places, the code index carrying a stale copy — are each on a ticket of their own and none is fixed inside this job.

decisions.title: A part of a file counts as a file when it weighs what a file weighs here
decisions.why: A share of the file would have refused most of the codebase, and a length would have refused the wrong things. What a file weighs is the one reading of enough that this codebase can answer itself: half of all files are lighter than the bar, and nothing crossed it in the last four hundred changes but one file since deleted.

decisions.title: The comparison decides on places refused, never on numbers moving
decisions.why: Watched pairs, counted parts and every size count rise on ordinary work; reading a rise as a decline made honest changes look like damage. A rule that counts downward says so by refusing, so the numbers can stay as context and nothing has to declare which way it counts.

decisions.title: The three files that already hold two things are excused, not split
decisions.why: Splitting them is a change to running code with its own risk, and it is not what this job was for. They are pinned by name to a ticket, the excuse list may only ever shrink, and the run reports any excuse that is no longer needed so the list cannot rot.

decisions.title: Every rule ships with a way to break it on purpose
decisions.why: A rule that passes is not evidence — the code it read may have been clean. Each rule is shown red with its fault put back and quiet with the fault fixed honestly, and that runs as a check rather than as something somebody once did. It caught one of my own rules going blind on the first run.

next.if_nothing: Nothing more happens. The suite runs on demand, refuses a change that made things worse, and the three excused files stay excused.

steps.step: The three files that hold two unrelated things each get split, so nothing is excused and the rule stands on its own
The copy numbers get re-read now that the measuring stick has shrunk
The engine moves to the shared home so every project gets it, with this project keeping only its own map and excuse lists
